newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania election exposes foreign policy rifts.
newsitem.headline: Romania election exposes foreign policy rifts.

text.p: Bitter arguments have burst out on the eve of Romania's presidential election over foreign policy, once an area of political accord in a country eagerly seeking NATO and European Union membership.

Ex-communist incumbent Ion Iliescu and his centrist challenger Emil Constantinescu clashed in their final television debate on Thursday over relations with Russia and the developing world and the effects of the Bosnian war.

Opposition politicians had largely backed Iliescu's mainly pro-Western policy and his drive to have Romania included in the first wave of NATO enlargement next year alongside more favoured candidates and to eventually win EU membership.

Constantinescu exploited Romania's drive for European integration -- surveys show the overwhelming majority of Romanians favour NATO membership -- to hammer home his central campaign plank that Romania is mired in economic crisis.
"NATO and the European Union are not charitable organisations. They don't accept countries that have not achieved minimum economic and social standards," he said.
"We are at the bottom of the list. We need a sound economy to support our integration."

But he saved his fiercest attack for policy towards the Kremlin, distrusted by the Balkan country even in communist times. He said it took the government until 1995, six years after the collapse of communism, to cancel accords authorising the deployment of Russian troops in Romania.
"Why did this take so long? By 1995, we were declaring our intention to join NATO," he said. "How could you possibly reconcile the two positions?"
Iliescu said the question was irrelevant as Soviet troops left Romania in 1951 and dictator Nicolae Ceausescu had opposed the Soviet Union for sending its forces into Czechoslovakia.
"There was never a danger that the Russians could come here over our heads," he said.
Why, Iliescu countered, had Constantinescu demanded a meeting of Romania's Security Council to discuss the Russian leader Boris Yeltsin's dismissal of top aide Alexander Lebed?

"There was surely no call to interfere in Russia's internal affairs," he said. "No one else reacted like this. This is a childish way to deal with foreign affairs for someone wanting to take on the job of head of state."

Constantinescu has never held high office and Iliescu has played on the danger of his inexperience. But Constantinescu has blasted Iliescu for stoking tension with ethnic Hungarians, a move sure to have irritated the Budapest government with which Romania signed a friendship treaty in September.
Iliescu said African embassies had blasted Constantinescu's allegation that corruption in the president's administration amounted to "turning Romania into an African country".

"What I meant by African was clear," Constantinescu protested. "I was referring to countries that are not yet democratic. A small minority with privileges and corruption, while the greater part of the population is poor."

Closer to home, Constantinescu said corrupt elements in Iliescu's government had exploited the U.N. embargo against rump Yugoslavia to amass fortunes in smuggling across the River Danube that separates the two countries.
"There was a mafia-like network making huge amounts by breaking the embargo," he said. Iliescu denied the allegations.
Constantinescu also reminded Iliescu of a statement at a conference earlier this year that Romania's only friends in the region were "Serbia and the Black Sea".
"Why don't you just admit you made a blunder?" he demanded. "Did you explain to the Greeks, for instance, that our only friends were the Serbs?"
